newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq denies U.S. plane attacked anti-aircraft site.
newsitem.headline: Iraq denies U.S. plane attacked anti-aircraft site.

text.p: Iraq's official news agency dismissed a Pentagon statement that a U.S. fighter plane had fired a missile against an Iraqi air defence site in southern Iraq on Monday as "groundless fabrication".
A Foreign Ministry source, quoted by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), linked the report -- the second of its kind in three days -- to the November 5 U.S. presidential election.
"Such allegations...are baseless as there has been no air activity of any kind in Iraq's airspace since noon today," the source said.
"Commenting on a similar news two days ago, we have stressed that such groundless fabrication of news is a means of election propaganda, American style," the source added.

In Washington, Defence Department spokesman Navy Cmdr. Joe March said: "An F-16 pilot assigned to the 4404th fighter wing fired a HARM (missile) after receiving an indication that his aircraft was being targeted by an Iraqi mobile surface-to-air system."
March said Monday's missile firing took place at about noon Iraq time (0900 GMT) about 25 miles (40 km) from where Saturday's incident occurred.

On Sunday Baghdad denied that any attack had taken place on Saturday. An Iraqi spokesman told INA that Iraq was still committed to a decision not to fire at U.S. and allied jets patrolling the two no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
The decision was taken in September after a confrontation with the United States because of Baghdad's backing of a Kurdish group in the north against a rival.

March said the F-16 returned to its base in the Gulf region safely after the Monday incident. He said there was no indication of damage to the missile site from the High-speed Anti-radiation Missile designed to seek out radar signals and destroy such sites.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry warned Iraq on Monday that U.S. jets would defend themselves, but the White House and Perry said there was no indication Iraq was playing a cat-and-mouse game with allied jets patrolling the no-fly zones.

"(Iraq's President) Saddam Hussein has very clear warning already from the fact that we conduct 100 sorties (flights) a day over this area" of southern Iraq, Perry told reporters in response to questions at the Pentagon.

The Defence Department had said on Sunday that the first U.S. attack, which occurred on Saturday in the same no-fly zone in southern Iraq, was a mistake because an investigation indicated Iraqi gunners had not targeted the F-16.
